title: Who holds the leash
hookLine: whoever controls what you want is your master (Enchiridion 14)
carry: the slack shows up at this end

lines: HOW MANY HANDS CAN TUG YOU?
cards: A phone buzzes on a table. Three people at dinner glance at it, including the person who swore they weren't going to. Somewhere, someone who designed that buzz is very pleased.

Here's a strange way to measure freedom: not by what you're allowed to do, but by how many hands can tug you. If anyone who can give or withhold what you badly want can move you, they have a kind of leash on you.
Epictetus spent his youth legally owned by another man. He knew what a master was.

teach.h: DON'T DEMAND WHAT NO ONE CAN PROMISE.
teach.b: Section fourteen of the handbook opens bluntly.

teach.h: YOUR MASTER: WHOEVER HOLDS WHAT YOU WANT.
teach.b: If you want your children and your partner and your friends to live forever, Epictetus says, you're being foolish: you want things that aren't up to you to be up to you.
If you want other people never to make mistakes, same problem. He isn't saying don't love them. He's saying don't demand what no one can promise.
Then the definition. Each person's master, he says, is whoever has the power to give or take away what that person wants or wants to avoid. That's the leash.

teach.h: WANT NOTHING THAT DEPENDS ON OTHERS.
teach.b: So whoever wants to be free, he says, should neither want nor avoid anything that depends on others. Otherwise, that person is bound to be a slave. It's a severe word, and he chose it knowing exactly what it meant.
Now look at what tugs a modern day: a boss's approval, a crush's reply, likes on a post, a parent's praise, a number on a scale. None of those people or things are bad.
But each time peace depends on them, someone is handed the end of a leash, often without asking for it.
Epictetus' point is that a lot of these leashes can be let go of from your end.
You can still want the reply. You can just stop needing it. The person holding the other end may never notice.
The slack shows up at this end.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism notice which wants make them dependent on others, such as approval or replies, and practice wanting them less urgently.

o: the student who wrote the Discourses down
a Stoic teacher, once enslaved, who taught freedom
the Roman emperor who wrote the Meditations

games.q: who holds the leash — tap the pairs.
p: wanting loved ones to live forever
wanting what isn't up to you
want nothing that depends on others

s: Epictetus says don't love your family
he says don't demand that they live forever; that isn't up to you.
Epictetus had been legally owned by another man
he chose the word slave knowing exactly what it meant.
section fourteen defines your master as whoever controls what you want or avoid

games.q: you want to be free in Epictetus' sense. what does section fourteen say to do?
o: gain power over the people around you.
want or avoid nothing that depends on others.
games.why: whoever wants to be free, he says, should neither want nor avoid what depends on others; otherwise they must be a slave.

practice: Picture your day as a field with a few leashes trailing from you, to a phone, a person's opinion, a number, and follow one to whoever holds the other end. Ask what you want from them that they can give or withhold.
Don't cut it; just loosen your own grip a little, and feel the slack.

wordCard.voice: Epictetus, once legally owned himself, measures freedom by who controls what you want or fear, until you let that want go. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Enchiridion 14: master, the one with authority.

carryVoice: Your line: the slack shows up at this end. Wanting the reply is fine; needing it is the leash. Until tomorrow.
